title: The Hidden Costs of Renting in India: What ₹25,000 Really Costs
seoTitle: Hidden Costs of Renting in India (2026)
description: Brokerage, maintenance, move-in charges, tanker water and the furnishing gap. What a rented flat in India really costs, and how to work it out first.
excerpt: The advertised rent is a headline, not a price. Here's every rupee that isn't rent — brokerage, maintenance, move-in charges, the furnishing gap — with a worked example of what a ₹25,000 flat actually costs.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters who have done this arithmetic too late

faq.q: Is brokerage compulsory when renting a flat in India?
faq.a: No. Brokerage is a fee for a service, not a legal requirement, and you only owe it if you used an agent and agreed to pay them. It is commonly quoted in months of rent, and how many months varies by city, by how tight the market is and by negotiation. If you find a home directly through the owner, there is no brokerage to pay at all.

faq.q: Who is supposed to pay society maintenance — the owner or the tenant?
faq.a: There is no universal rule; it is whatever the two of you agree and write into the agreement. In many arrangements the tenant pays the monthly maintenance while the owner covers capital items like the sinking fund or corpus contribution. Because it can add thousands of rupees a month, settle it in writing before signing rather than assuming. Ask for the last two maintenance bills so you know the real figure and how it is calculated.

faq.q: Why is my electricity bill so much higher than a friend’s for similar usage?
faq.a: Usually one of three reasons. The connection may be billed at a commercial rather than domestic tariff, which uses different slabs. The meter may be a society sub-meter billed at the society’s own rate rather than the utility’s. Or you may be paying a fixed generator-backup charge on top of consumption. Ask which arrangement applies and look at two actual past bills before you sign.

faq.q: What does "unfurnished" actually include in an Indian rental?
faq.a: Often very little. An unfurnished flat can arrive with no wardrobes, no lights or fans, no geyser, no chimney or hob and no curtain rods — walls, floors, plumbing points and electrical points. "Semi-furnished" has no fixed definition and means whatever the owner thinks it means. Walk through and write down item by item what is actually there before you budget.

faq.q: How much should I budget over and above the advertised rent?
faq.a: There is no reliable national figure, and anyone quoting one is guessing. The honest approach is to build your own number: add maintenance, parking, expected electricity, any water share and internet to the rent for the monthly total, then separately add deposit, brokerage, move-in charges, agreement costs, furnishing and moving for the upfront total. Do it for each flat you are considering and compare those totals rather than the rents.

faq.q: Do I have to pay brokerage again when I renew my agreement?
faq.a: Not automatically. A renewal between you and the owner needs no agent, so there is nothing to pay. Some owners work through an agent for renewals and pass on a fee, and some agreements mention it — check before the eleventh month rather than during it. You may still face fresh stamp duty and registration on the new agreement, plus any escalation clause.

body:
The flat was advertised at ₹25,000 a month. Meera had budgeted ₹30,000, so she moved in feeling comfortable. A little headroom, even.

Three weeks later she added it up properly on the back of a delivery bill, because the money was going faster than it should have been.

Brokerage: one month's rent, paid the day she got the keys. Deposit: five months, gone in a single transfer. Maintenance, which the owner had mentioned once, quickly, near the door — ₹3,200 a month, and no, not included. A ₹5,000 move-in charge the society collected before the lift could be used for furniture. A tempo and two men on a Saturday. Then curtain rods, four tube lights, a fan for the second bedroom and a geyser, because *unfurnished* in India means something very specific and quite literal.

Her first month cost a little over two lakh rupees. Her steady monthly cost, once the summer electricity bill arrived and the water tanker had come for the third time in June, sat closer to ₹32,000 than ₹25,000.

Nothing had been hidden from her, exactly. Nobody lied. Nobody had ever put the whole number in one place — including, honestly, the owner.

## The advertised rent is a headline, not a price

Rent gets advertised because rent is what gets compared. Every listing, every broker's forwarded photo set, every board outside a building leads with it. So that's the number that lodges in your head, and that's what your budget gets built around.

The problem is that rent is one line in a bill with about a dozen lines.

Some of the others are monthly and permanent. Some are one-time and large. Several depend entirely on the building — one society charges nothing to move in, the next wants ₹10,000 and a form signed by a committee member. A few depend on the season, because water in an Indian April is not the same commodity it is in November.

Two flats advertised at the same rent can cost you ₹5,000 a month apart. That happens constantly. It isn't deception; the information just isn't collected anywhere, so nobody has the total in front of them.

So let's collect it.

## Brokerage: the biggest number, for the least work

Brokerage in India is usually quoted in months of rent. How many months varies by city, by how tight the local market is, by whether the agent is working for the owner or for you, and — this matters more than people expect — by whether you ask.

What does it buy? Sometimes a genuinely useful person: someone who knows the building, filters out the listings that would waste your Saturday, and gets the owner to actually answer the phone. Sometimes a phone number, a set of keys, and an afternoon.

Either way it's paid upfront, in full, and it isn't refundable. It doesn't reduce your rent by a rupee. And on the standard eleven-month cycle it isn't really a one-time cost across a renting life — it's a recurring one with a long gap.

Get the amount agreed in writing before any viewing, not after you've fallen for a flat. And be careful of anyone asking for money before you've seen the property or met the owner — that pattern shows up constantly in [rental scams](/blog/rental-scams-in-india).

## Maintenance: the charge that hides in plain sight

Society or association maintenance is the single most commonly under-asked number in Indian renting, and it's charged two completely different ways.

**Flat rate.** Every flat in the building pays the same, say ₹2,500 a month, regardless of size.

**Per square foot.** You pay a rate multiplied by your flat's area. At ₹3 per square foot, a 1,050 sq ft flat is ₹3,150 a month — and a bigger flat in the same building pays proportionally more.

Neither is unfair. But if you don't ask which one applies, you can't estimate anything, and the difference between the two on a large flat is real money.

Then ask what it covers — lift and pump electricity, common lighting, security and housekeeping are typical, while a gym or pool pushes it up. Some societies bill quarterly, so it lands as a lump every three months.

And ask who pays it. In some arrangements the owner absorbs maintenance; in many the tenant pays. It's negotiable, it changes your monthly cost significantly, and it belongs in the agreement in plain words rather than agreed in a hallway. The sinking fund or corpus contribution is usually the owner's — that's a capital contribution to the building, not a service you're consuming.

The most useful request you can make: *can I see the last two maintenance bills?* An actual bill settles all of this at once.

## The deposit's real cost is the money standing still

Deposits vary wildly across India. Some cities settle around two or three months, others routinely ask for far more. Whatever your number, the cost most people miss isn't that the money leaves — most of it comes back.

The cost is that it sits there doing nothing.

For however long you live in that flat, a large sum is unavailable to you. It isn't your emergency fund. It isn't earning you anything. And it can't be the deposit on your next flat until this one is refunded — which is exactly why so many renters end up borrowing to move.

Think of it as rent you pay on your own money. If a big deposit is the price of a slightly lower monthly rent, do that arithmetic over the real length of your stay rather than assuming the lower rent wins.

The law around deposits and how to actually get yours returned is a subject of its own — we've covered it in [security deposits in India](/blog/security-deposits-in-india). Here the point is simply: budget for it as money you won't see again for years, because functionally that's what it is.

## The one-time charges that appear at the door

These ambush people, because they arrive after you've committed and they aren't in any listing.

- **Society move-in charge.** A non-refundable admin fee some associations levy on a new tenant — a few hundred rupees, or several thousand.
- **Lift or shifting charges.** Some societies charge per trip to use the lift for furniture. Some ban it entirely, which means stairs, and stairs mean higher labour charges from your movers.
- **Move-in timing rules.** No shifting on Sundays, nothing after 6pm, nothing during festival week. Trivial until they cost you a day of leave.
- **Society paperwork.** Forms, an NOC, sometimes a file charge, often police verification.
- **Stamp duty and registration** on the agreement, which varies by state. Who pays is negotiable and often split — settle it before signing, not at the sub-registrar's office.
- **New connection and transfer charges.** Gas connection transfer, internet installation, a router deposit, sometimes an electricity name-transfer or fresh connection deposit.

None is huge alone. Together they routinely exceed a month's rent.

## Electricity and water: same flat, very different bills

Electricity is where two identical flats diverge most sharply.

**Tariff type.** Domestic and commercial tariffs are different, and not by a little. In some mixed-use buildings, or where a flat is registered under a commercial connection, you can end up billed at commercial slabs for a home. Ask what the connection is.

**Separate meter or shared?** A dedicated meter in your name, billed by the utility, is the clean case. A sub-meter read by the society and billed at the society's own rate is common — and that rate isn't always the utility's. Some buildings add a handling markup. Not automatically wrong, but you should know it's happening.

**DG backup.** Generator backup is usually a fixed monthly charge plus a per-unit rate for what you draw. In cities with frequent cuts that's a real line item, not a rounding error.

Ask to see two actual bills, ideally one from summer and one from winter. Nothing else you can ask replaces that.

Water is the other seasonal one. Where municipal supply is short, societies buy tankers and split the cost across flats — noticeable for a few months, near zero the rest of the year. Ask where the water actually comes from, and whether tanker charges are shared per flat or per head.

## Parking, and other things sold separately

Parking is frequently not included in rent. It might be a separate monthly charge, it might be allocated by the society and simply unavailable, and two-wheelers and cars are usually priced differently. If there's no parking, the cost doesn't vanish — it becomes a paid spot nearby, or street parking and the risk that goes with it. Some societies also make a clubhouse membership compulsory. Worth asking rather than discovering.

## The furnishing gap

This one catches people moving within India as much as people moving to it.

"Unfurnished" here can mean genuinely bare. No wardrobes. No lights or fans. No geyser. No chimney or hob. No curtain rods. Sometimes no cabinets under the kitchen platform. You are renting walls, a floor, plumbing points and electrical points.

"Semi-furnished" has no fixed definition at all. It means whatever the owner thinks it means, which might be wardrobes and fans, or might be a single ceiling fan in one room.

Filling that gap is real money, and most of it doesn't come back — you either leave it behind or pay to dismantle and move it. So walk through and write down, item by item, what's actually there: wardrobes, fans, lights, geyser, chimney, hob, exhaust fans, curtain rods, kitchen cabinets, AC units and whether they work.

That list does double duty. It's your furnishing budget, and it's exactly the inventory you want signed when you move in.

## Painting, renewal, and the costs that come back around

Many agreements include a repainting clause: the flat is repainted at your cost when you vacate, or a fixed amount is deducted for it. Sometimes it's a specific figure. Sometimes it's "as per actuals", which is a blank cheque. Read it before you sign, not on the way out — this and the other clauses that bite at exit are covered in [rental agreements in India](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india).

Most Indian agreements also run for eleven months, for registration reasons rather than any natural rhythm, so renewal arrives fast. At renewal you may face an escalation clause raising the rent, fresh stamp duty and registration on the new agreement, and — if the owner works through an agent — sometimes a renewal brokerage. Budget for your rent rising on a schedule.

## Moving itself

Packers and movers, or a tempo plus two men and a lost weekend. The price swings hugely on distance, floor, whether the lift can be used, and how much you own.

The line people forget: air conditioners. Dismantling, transporting, a gas refill and reinstalling at the new place is a proper cost, separate from the tempo. Add cleaning, half a day of carpentry, and the hardware run that every move somehow requires.

## A worked example

Take an invented but unremarkable example — a two-bedroom flat advertised at ₹25,000 a month, deposit five months, brokerage one month, maintenance at ₹3 per square foot on 1,050 sq ft.

**These are made-up round figures chosen to show the shape of the bill.** They are not averages, not market rates, and not research. Your city, your building and your negotiation will all differ. The point is the arithmetic, not the numbers.

| What you pay | One-time (₹) | Every month (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rent | 25,000 (first month) | 25,000 |
| Security deposit (5 months) | 1,25,000 | — |
| Brokerage (1 month) | 25,000 | — |
| Society maintenance (₹3/sq ft) | — | 3,150 |
| Society move-in + lift charge | 5,000 | — |
| Stamp duty and registration (split) | 3,000 | — |
| Electricity incl. DG backup | — | 2,200 |
| Water tanker share (summer months) | — | 600 |
| Parking, one car | — | 1,000 |
| Internet install + router deposit | 2,500 | 800 |
| Gas connection transfer | 1,000 | — |
| Furnishing gap: geyser, lights, fans, rods, one wardrobe | 32,000 | — |
| Tempo, labour, AC shifting | 14,000 | — |
| **Total** | **2,32,500** | **32,750** |

Read the two columns separately, because they hurt differently.

The monthly column is the one you live with: ₹32,750 against an advertised ₹25,000, roughly 31% more than the number that got you through the door. If you'd budgeted ₹30,000, this flat is quietly over budget forever.

The one-time column empties an account. Of that ₹2,32,500, the ₹1,25,000 deposit should come back eventually. The remaining ₹1,07,500 is simply spent — more than four months of the advertised rent, gone before you've slept there a night.

### Now compare two homes properly

Same illustrative spirit, two flats you might genuinely be choosing between:

| | Flat A | Flat B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Advertised rent | 25,000 | 27,000 |
| Maintenance | 3,150 | included |
| Parking | 1,000 | included |
| Electricity (shared meter vs own domestic meter) | 3,400 | 2,000 |
| Water tanker share | 600 | 0 |
| **True monthly cost** | **33,150** | **29,000** |

Flat B is advertised ₹2,000 higher and costs ₹4,150 a month less. Over an eleven-month agreement that's more than ₹45,000.

If you compare on rent, you pick the wrong flat. Confidently.

## The mistakes that cost the most

**Budgeting against the advertised rent.** Everything above follows from this one.

**Not asking who pays maintenance, or how it's calculated.** Two questions, thirty seconds, thousands of rupees.

**Accepting "all inclusive" without a list.** Inclusive of what? Get the items named.

**Ignoring the tariff type and meter arrangement.** This is the difference that shows up every single month.

**Treating one-time costs as trivial because they're one-time.** They aren't trivial, and on an eleven-month cycle they aren't really one-time either.

**Underestimating the furnishing gap.** People budget a few thousand and spend thirty.

**Never asking about exit costs.** Repainting, restoration, notice period. You'll meet them when your bargaining power is at its lowest.

**Forgetting the commute.** A flat ₹2,000 cheaper and 12 km further out can cost more than it saves in fuel, cabs and hours — one reason [maps beat lists for finding a home](/blog/why-maps-beat-lists-for-finding-a-home).

## How to ask, before you commit

Send it as one message, so the answers exist in writing. Owners generally answer this fine — it reads as organised, not suspicious.

1. Is maintenance included in the rent? If not, how much, how is it calculated, and who pays it?
2. Can I see the last two maintenance bills and two electricity bills?
3. Is there a move-in charge or a lift/shifting charge from the society?
4. Is the electricity meter separate and on the domestic tariff, or billed through the society?
5. Is DG backup charged separately, and how?
6. Where does the water come from, and are tanker charges shared?
7. Is parking included, and for how many vehicles?
8. What exactly is in the flat — wardrobes, geyser, lights, fans, chimney, exhaust fans?
9. Is repainting on exit charged to me, and at what rate?
10. Who pays stamp duty and registration, and what's the renewal escalation?

Ten questions, about four minutes of the owner's time, and the highest-return four minutes in the whole process. There's a longer version in [questions to ask before renting](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting), and the viewing-day version in the [house-hunting checklist](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india).

## Compare on true cost, not rent

The habit to build is one line of arithmetic, done for every flat before you shortlist it:

> **True monthly = rent + maintenance + parking + expected electricity + water share + internet**

Then a separate figure for getting in the door: deposit + brokerage + move-in charges + agreement costs + furnishing gap + moving.

Write both beside each flat's name. Two minutes per property, and it reorders your shortlist more than any viewing will.

## Where StayOnMap fits, honestly

We can't make a society drop its move-in charge, and we have no idea what your tanker bill will be in May.

What we did do is make the numbers visible before you go and look. Every listing states rent, deposit and maintenance as required fields — an owner can't post without them — along with any other charges. So the figures you need to compare two homes are on the card, not sprung on you in a hallway after you've mentally moved in.

There's also no brokerage on [StayOnMap](https://www.stayonmap.com) at all. Not a reduced rate, none — you contact the owner directly. Since brokerage is usually the largest one-time cost in the whole list above, removing it does more for your first-month total than anything else we could build.

The rest of the questions still have to be asked. But you can ask them of the person who actually knows the answers, before you spend a Saturday crossing the city to find out.

## What to remember

The advertised rent is a headline. The true monthly cost is rent plus maintenance plus parking plus electricity plus water plus internet — and it lands meaningfully above the listing figure far more often than not.

The one-time cost is bigger still, and most of it — brokerage, move-in charges, furnishing, moving — never comes back. Only the deposit does, eventually, after sitting idle for years.

Ask ten questions before you commit. Ask for two real bills. Compare flats on the total, not the headline.

Meera stayed in that flat two years and liked it. But when she moved, she did it differently: before visiting anything, she asked every owner the same ten questions and wrote two numbers beside each address.

The place she picked was advertised ₹1,500 higher than her second choice. It's costing her ₹3,000 a month less.
